_comment: The syscalls buildclamp's sandbox issues that a restrictive container seccomp profile
is likely to refuse. This is NOT a complete profile: it is the delta, to be merged
into whatever profile your runtime already applies, by ops/make-seccomp-profile.sh.
Why a delta and not a whole profile. A container's default profile is an ALLOWLIST of
around three hundred syscall names, and a copy of it that this project maintained by
hand would be wrong in the direction that breaks containers: one name missing and an
unrelated program in the image stops working, with an EPERM that names nothing. The
authoritative copy is the one your runtime ships. This file says what to add to it.
Every entry below was read out of crates/sandbox/src, not out of a specification:
is the check, and ops/make-seccomp-profile.sh runs it so that a syscall added to the
sandbox and not to this file fails CI rather than a customer's container.

additions.why: creates the user, mount and network namespaces. Docker's default profile permits the name; several hardened profiles and some managed node images do not, and a profile that permits `unshare` only with no namespace flags is the same as not permitting it here.

the fork between installing the namespace and applying the seccomp filter. Docker's default profile allows `clone` only when NO namespace flag is set and returns ENOSYS for `clone3` without CAP_SYS_ADMIN; buildclamp does not pass namespace flags to clone — it unshares first — but glibc's `fork` reaches `clone3` on current versions, so a profile that ENOSYSes it forces the slower path or fails outright.

the read-only root. All three run INSIDE the new mount namespace, where they affect nothing outside the container — but a seccomp profile is applied per task and cannot tell the two cases apart, so it has to permit them.
installs the filter that refuses or records a unit's syscalls. Without it nothing below the namespace tier works at all, and `doctor` reports `seccomp notification: no`.

PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS, which the kernel requires before an unprivileged process may install a seccomp filter. Almost every profile already permits it; it is listed because omitting it makes the seccomp tier fail with EACCES rather than with anything that names the cause.
SECCOMP_IOCTL_NOTIF_RECV, _SEND and _ID_VALID — the supervisor's whole conversation with the kernel. Profiles that permit `ioctl` only for a named set of requests will refuse these three.
drops the capabilities the new user namespace hands the child, so a unit does not run with a full capability set inside its own namespace.

the filesystem tier. These are newer than most published profiles, and a profile whose default action is ERRNO refuses every syscall it has never heard of — so on such a host Landlock reports absent when the kernel has it. That is the single most common way a container reports a weaker tier than its kernel can provide, and it looks identical to an old kernel.
